newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan urges Israel to keep Mideast peace alive.
newsitem.headline: Jordan urges Israel to keep Mideast peace alive.

text.p: Jordan on Monday urged Israel to keep peace talks with the Palestinians alive, saying the alternative would be a "catastrophe" for the whole region.

"This is a matter, we pray to God, will not happen because the alternative is a catastrophe for the whole region...We do not accept this talk (of ending the peace talks)," Foreign Minister Fayez al-Tarawnah told Reuters ahead of a meeting later on Monday between King Hussein and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat.
"There is a great and pressing need for joint efforts to keep the peace process alive," he also added after a meeting with Israeli parliamentarians.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was quoted on Sunday as saying that Israel would not honour peace deals it signed with Arafat unless the Palestinian president cracked down on Islamic radicals.

Tarawnah said the suicide bombings, which killed 13 people in a Jewish market in Jerusalem last Wednesday, should only toughen the resolve of the parties to the conflict to get the peace process back on track.
He said that King Hussein would discuss with Arafat later in the day in Amman ways of defusing the deepening crisis in Israeli-Palestinian ties which worsened after the latest suicide bombings.
Officials earlier said Arafat would seek King Hussein's support in the face of Israeli pressure on him after Wednesday's bombings.
They privately expressed their support of the Palestinian leader's view that the bombings were being exploited by Israel to backtrack on peace commitments.

Jordan was also working with Washington to formulate an initiative which could be the basis for the resumption of stalled peace talks, ahead of a visit by U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross to the region to try to defuse growing tension, Tarawnah added.

Tarawnah attacked Israel for taking tough security measures against the Palestinians in the fight against Moslem militants following the bombings, saying such steps were counterproductive and hindered the ability of Palestinians to stem terrorism.
The king has said the bloodshed could have been precipitated by growing frustrations with a stalled peace process and anger over an accelerated Jewish settlement drive in the West Bank.

"Peace is in essence security, but there are other dimensions aside from security which should be taken into account, which relate directly to Palestinian rights and their aspirations from peace," Tarawnah added, saying Israel should treat the Palestinian Authority as a partner not an enemy.
King Hussein has expressed increasing exasperation with Netanyahu's policies, publicly doubting his resolve to advance the peace process.
On Sunday he again expressed his deep concern over the fate of the peace process.
"We have to move quickly and with determination to rectify the peace path before it is too late," he told the delegation of Israeli Knesset (parliament) members.

Jordan is worried by the repercussions of renewed violence in Palestinian territories on its own stability. The kingdom's 4.2 million people have close ethnic ties with Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.
